hints: Think about why a non-polar $\text{Br}_2$ molecule becomes polar when it approaches the high electron density of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond.
Remember that in electrophilic addition the $\pi$ electrons act as the nucleophile and attack the slightly positive end of the electrophile.
Consider what intermediate forms after one $\text{C-Br}$ bond is made and what nucleophile attacks it in the second step.
walkthrough:
Make bromine into an electrophile**
Picture ethene with its exposed $\pi$ electron cloud approaching $\text{Br}_2$. The electron cloud repels the electrons in $\text{Br}_2$, so the $\text{Br}$ atom nearer the double bond becomes $\delta+$ and the further one becomes $\delta-$. Write it as $\text{Br}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$. That induced dipole is what allows a non-polar molecule to be attacked.

Attack by the double bond**
The $\text{C}=\text{C}$ $\pi$ bond is electron rich, so it donates a pair to $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$. Draw a curly arrow starting in the middle of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond and pointing to the $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$. At the same time the $\text{Br}-\text{Br}$ bond breaks, so draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{Br}-\text{Br}$ bond onto the $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ to give $\text{Br}^{-}$. One carbon now bonds to Br, the other becomes $\text{C}^{+}$, giving $\text{CH}_2^{+}\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$.

Capture of the carbocation**
The positively charged carbon is strongly electron deficient. The $\text{Br}^{-}$ formed has full lone pairs, so it donates one pair to $\text{C}^{+}$. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{Br}^{-}$ to the $\text{C}^{+}$ centre. This forms the second $\text{C-Br}$ bond and gives 1,2-dibromoethane, $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$.

Final answer: First step: $\text{Br}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ shown with curly arrow from $\text{C}=\text{C}$ to $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$ and curly arrow from $\text{Br}-\text{Br}$ bond to $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ to give carbocation $\text{CH}_2^{+}\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$.
Second step: curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{Br}^{-}$ to $\text{C}^{+}$ to give $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$.

hints: Write the expression $\Delta H_r = \Sigma \Delta H_f(\text{products}) - \Sigma \Delta H_f(\text{reactants})$ for reaction 1 and remember $\Delta H_f(\text{Br}_2) = 0$ as an element.
walkthrough:
Link formation data to reaction enthalpy**
For $\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$:
$$\Delta H_r = \Delta H_f(\text{product}) - [\Delta H_f(\text{ethene}) + \Delta H_f(\text{Br}_2)]$$
Since $\text{Br}_2$ is an element in its standard state, its $\Delta H_f = 0$. Rearranging:
$$\Delta H_f(\text{product}) = \Delta H_r + \Delta H_f(\text{ethene})$$
$$= -90.0 + (+52.2) = -37.8\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Final answer: $\Delta H_f \text{ of 1,2-dibromoethane} = -37.8\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Compare reaction 2 with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ to reaction 3 with $\text{NaOH}$ in ethanol, recall which condition gives substitution and which gives elimination.
For reaction 2 both $\text{Br}$ atoms are replaced by $\text{OH}$, while for reaction 3 only $\text{HBr}$ is lost to form a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond.
walkthrough:
Sort out substitution versus elimination**
Aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ favours nucleophilic substitution of bromoalkane to alcohol. Ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$ favours elimination of $\text{HBr}$ to form an alkene. So reaction 2 must give a diol and reaction 3 must give an unsaturated bromide.

Draw A and name B**
Starting from $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, replace each $\text{Br}$ by $\text{OH}$ to get $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ for A. Remove one $\text{H}$ and one $\text{Br}$ to get $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHBr}$, which is bromoethene for B.

Final answer: A is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, ethane-1,2-diol.
B is bromoethene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHBr}$.

hints: Visualise the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ of bromoethene opening to a single bond that links to neighbours on both sides.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond**
Addition polymerisation simply joins many $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHBr}$ molecules by converting the double bond to single bonds. Draw $\text{-CH}_2-\text{CH(Br)-}$ with a continuation bond at each end to show it repeats. The Br stays attached to every second carbon.
Final answer: Repeat unit: $\text{-[CH}_2-\text{CHBr]-}$ with continuation bonds through the carbons.

hints: Excess hot ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$ removes $\text{HBr}$ twice from $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHBr}$, leaving only carbon and hydrogen in an unsaturated hydrocarbon.
walkthrough:
Lose HBr completely**
Bromoethene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHBr}$, with excess ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$ undergoes further elimination. Removing H from one carbon and Br from the other creates a triple bond. The only hydrocarbon left with two carbons is $\text{HC}\equiv\text{CH}$, formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2$.
Final answer: D is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2$, ethyne ($\text{HC}\equiv\text{CH}$).

hints: Compare $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ with $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBr}_2$, the carbon skeleton is the same but the Br positions differ.
walkthrough:
Check the type of isomerism**
Both compounds have molecular formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{Br}_2$ but the Br atoms are on different carbons, 1,2 versus 1,1. Same skeleton, different position of functional group, so this is structural, positional isomerism.
Final answer: Structural (positional) isomerism.

hints: Look at the $\text{-CHO}$ group in F, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$, and recall which homologous series contains the terminal $\text{C}=\text{O}$ with H.
walkthrough:
Recognise the functional group**
F is $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$ with $\text{C}=\text{O}$ at the end of the chain bonded to H. That $\text{-CHO}$ group defines the aldehydes.
Final answer: Aldehyde.

hints: Recall the general test for any carbonyl compound with $\text{C}=\text{O}$ using 2,4-DNPH.
Think about how Tollens reagent distinguishes aldehydes like ethanal from ketones.
Remember that ethanal contains a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ group, so consider the iodoform reaction with alkaline $\text{I}_2$.
walkthrough:
Test for carbonyl**
F is ethanal, an aldehyde, so it contains $\text{C}=\text{O}$. With 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine it forms a yellow, orange or red precipitate of the hydrazone. This is positive for both aldehydes and ketones.

Confirm aldehyde with Tollens**
Tollens reagent oxidises aldehydes but not ketones. Ethanal reduces $\text{Ag}^{+}$ to Ag metal, giving the classic silver mirror on the tube wall, seen as a grey to black precipitate if not clean.

Confirm methyl carbonyl with iodoform**
Ethanal has the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ unit, so with alkaline $\text{I}_2(\text{aq})$ warmed it gives the iodoform reaction, forming yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_3$ with antiseptic smell.

Final answer: 2,4-DNPH: yellow / orange / red precipitate.
Tollens reagent: silver mirror (or grey / black precipitate).
Alkaline $\text{I}_2(\text{aq})$: yellow precipitate.

hints: Use the molecular ion at $m/e = 60$ to get the $M_r$ and think which oxidation product of ethanal has that mass.
Look for the very broad absorption around $3000-2500\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ in Fig. 4.3 and match it in Table 4.2.
Check the strong sharp absorption near $1700\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ and the absorption in the $1040-1300\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ region to confirm the second oxygen functional group.
walkthrough:
Start from mass and chemistry**
F is $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$. Oxidation adds O to give $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ with $M_r = 60$, exactly matching the molecular ion at $m/e = 60$. That is a strong clue that H is ethanoic acid.

Spot the carboxylic O-H**
In Fig. 4.3 there is a very broad dip centred near $3000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ extending down to $2500\ \text{cm}^{-1}$. Table 4.2 shows carboxyl O-H absorbs at $2500-3000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$. The breadth is characteristic of hydrogen bonded carboxylic acids, different from a sharper alcohol O-H.

Confirm C=O and C-O**
There is a strong sharp absorption near $1700\ \text{cm}^{-1}$, matching C=O in the range $1670-1740\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ for carbonyl / carboxyl. There is also absorption in the $1040-1300\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ fingerprint region matching C-O of hydroxy / ester / acid. Together with $M_r = 60$, only $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ fits all three pieces of evidence.

Final answer: H is $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, ethanoic acid.
Broad absorption in range $2500-3000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ shows O-H of carboxyl group.
Absorption in range $1670-1750\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ shows C=O and / or absorption in $1040-1300\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ shows C-O, combined with $M_r = 60$ from $M^{+}$ at $m/e = 60$.

hints: Consider the change from $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$ to $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, whether oxygen is gained and what type of reagent causes that.
walkthrough:
Identify the role**
Converting an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid gains oxygen, which is oxidation. So G must act as an oxidising agent, for example acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ or Tollens type oxidation under suitable conditions.
Final answer: Oxidising agent (oxidant).
